I don't know why I'm taking this seriously, but:

Let's say a factory needs 6 operators on a line which produces widgets. The process is a bit complicated, hence needing 6 operators. Yet, it's a decently fast machine, and stamps out 1,000 widgets an hour, 24 hours a day.

Now, Let's say these operators are making a decent wage, and once their benefits are included, the company is paying out $28/hr.

How much more does each widget cost? Approximately 17¢ additional.

If you were to purchase 3 products per day, every day, all year, the passed along cost (vs. ZERO labor costs) would be just over $185.

Now, as a corporation, especially a gigantic one, you see this 17¢ multiplied day after day after day so it adds up to become a very large number. So you pillage your country to make corporate profit for those at the top and those who own shares.

I am a new product developer with two bachelors degrees (mechanical engineering and manufacturing engineering) and I work at a factory. The reason that factories are economic engines is because they have to have other companies to support what they do. If a factory makes televisions, then that factory needs to have several different companies to supply all of the components to make those televisions, such as semiconductors, injection molded plastic, glass, etc. The smaller companies then need to have suppliers of their own, and if there are several suppliers available then that gives the potential for another company to make televisions and give competition for the initial television factory to keep all of the supply chains at full capacity. Manufacturing jobs create a multiplier effect for the economy.

Most manufacturing jobs also have labor unions, which provide high wages and health benefits for their workers. I have worked in union shops and non-union shops and they both have their up and downs, but providing workers with good pay and benefits tend to make the surrounding areas a nicer place for all people.

Manufacturing jobs also lead to innovation as the market is always hungry for new and better products. Many manufacturers have R&D to provide facilities to create these products and the people who work there work and live as research students but for the purpose of learning for the benefit of profits. The issue with university innovation is that it is lengthy, most likely requires government grants or public funding, and does not generate profits by itself, so by having manufacturers to offer these ideas or process improvements to schools can become a lot stronger and companies can make more profit. School and work go hand in hand.
